group.passage: We see these small symbols every day on keyboards, screens, and packages, but few of us know where they came from. Some are hundreds of years old, while others appeared only a few decades ago. Here are the stories behind six of them.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: The At Sign (@)
passage_parts.text: Hundreds of years ago, merchants in Italy used @ in their business records. In 1971, Ray Tomlinson, an engineer, was building a way to send messages between computers. He needed a mark to separate a person’s name from the computer’s name, and he chose @ because it was not often used.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: The Ampersand (&)
passage_parts.text: The & sign began as a quick way to write et, the Latin word for “and.” Writers would join the two letters into one shape. In the early 1800s, children ended the alphabet with it, saying “and per se and,” or “and, by itself, and.” Said quickly, these words became “ampersand.”

passage_parts.label: C
passage_parts.title: The Hash Sign (#)
passage_parts.text: For a long time, # was simply called the number sign. Then in 2007, Chris Messina suggested on Twitter that people type # before a word to mark posts on the same topic. Later that year, people used it to share news about a big fire in San Diego, and the idea quickly caught on.

passage_parts.label: D
passage_parts.title: The Power Symbol
passage_parts.text: The power button on your phone shows a short line and a circle. The line stands for 1, which means “on,” and the circle stands for 0, which means “off.” The symbol first appeared in a set of international standards in 1973. At first, it meant a kind of sleep mode, but today most people simply read it as “power.”

passage_parts.label: E
passage_parts.title: The Recycling Symbol
passage_parts.text: In 1970, a company that made paper boxes held a contest for the first Earth Day. Design students across the country were invited to create a symbol for recycled paper. The contest was won by Gary Anderson, a college student in California, who drew three bent arrows that form a loop.

passage_parts.label: F
passage_parts.title: The Smiley :-)
passage_parts.text: In 1982, Scott Fahlman, a researcher at Carnegie Mellon University, noticed a problem on the school’s online message board. People often missed the jokes in other people’s posts and took them seriously. He suggested typing :-) after a joke. Tilt your head to the left, and you will see a smiling face.

translation_zh.text:
我們每天都會在鍵盤、螢幕和包裝上看到這些小符號，但很少人知道它們是從哪裡來的。有些已經有幾百年的歷史，有些則是幾十年前才出現。以下是其中六個符號背後的故事。
A 小老鼠（@）：幾百年前，義大利的商人就在帳冊上使用 @。1971 年，工程師雷‧湯林森（Ray Tomlinson）正在建立一種在電腦之間傳送訊息的方法。他需要一個符號，把使用者的名字和電腦的名稱分開，於是選了 @，因為這個符號不常被使用。
B 「&」符號（ampersand）：& 最初是快速書寫 et 的寫法，et 是拉丁文的「和」。書寫者會把這兩個字母連成一個形狀。1800 年代初期，孩子背字母表時會以它結尾，唸成「and per se and」，也就是「and，單獨一個字就是 and」。這幾個字唸快了，就變成了「ampersand」。
C 井字號（#）：很長一段時間，# 只被叫做「數字符號」。後來在 2007 年，克里斯‧梅西納（Chris Messina）在推特上建議大家在一個詞前面打上 #，用來標記同一主題的貼文。同一年稍晚，大家用它分享聖地牙哥一場大火的消息，這個點子很快就流行起來。
D 電源符號：你手機上的電源鍵畫著一條短線和一個圓圈。線代表 1，意思是「開」；圓圈代表 0，意思是「關」。這個符號在 1973 年首次出現在一套國際標準中。起初它代表一種睡眠模式，但現在大多數人直接把它看成「電源」。
E 回收標誌：1970 年，一家製造紙箱的公司為第一屆世界地球日舉辦了一場比賽，邀請全國各地學設計的學生為再生紙設計一個標誌。贏得比賽的是加州的大學生蓋瑞‧安德森（Gary Anderson），他畫了三個彎折的箭頭，圍成一個循環。
F 笑臉 :-)：1982 年，卡內基美隆大學的研究人員史考特‧法爾曼（Scott Fahlman）注意到學校線上留言板的一個問題：大家常常看不出別人貼文裡的玩笑，而把它們當真。他建議在玩笑後面打上 :-)。把頭往左邊歪，你就會看到一張笑臉。
